criteria.descriptor: Correctly explains that open/unpinned constraints cause pip to resolve to different versions at install time — including transitive dependencies — and accurately distinguishes a manifest (intent/ranges) from a lockfile (exact resolved tree, typically with hashes). Names real, correctly-described tooling (pip-tools/pip-compile, Poetry+poetry.lock, uv+uv.lock, Pipfile.lock, --require-hashes) with no factual errors such as claiming version ranges lock a build.

Addresses all three parts: root cause, manifest-vs-lockfile distinction, and a concrete reproducibility fix that includes both generating AND committing the lockfile plus installing from it. Full marks also surface the transitive-dependency point and separate upgrading (re-lock) from installing.

Explains WHY a committed lockfile guarantees an identical tree (every version — ideally hash — is fixed so the resolver has no freedom, and CI/teammates stop resolving independently), rather than merely naming a tool to adopt.

A clear, well-organised explanation using correct vocabulary (pinning, transitive dependency, reproducible build, lockfile, resolver) that a teammate could act on directly, with the three asked-for parts easy to locate.

expected_answer_points: Root cause: unpinned constraints make pip re-resolve to the latest satisfying versions at install time, so different machines/times get different versions — a non-reproducible build.
Identifies that the failing library is a transitive (indirect) dependency, so pinning only direct packages is insufficient; the entire dependency graph must be fixed.
Manifest = declares intent/direct deps and version ranges for humans (pyproject.toml, requirements.in); lockfile = records exact resolved versions of the full tree (often with hashes) for machines.
Concrete fix names real lockfile tooling: Poetry (poetry.lock), uv (uv.lock), pip-tools/pip-compile, or Pipenv (Pipfile.lock), installing via poetry install / uv sync / pip install --require-hashes.
The lockfile must be committed to version control so teammates and CI install from it rather than re-resolving independently.
Justifies reproducibility: with every version (and hash) pinned there is nothing left for the resolver to choose, and hashes add integrity; upgrading is a separate, reviewable re-lock step.
common_pitfalls: Pins only the direct packages (fastapi==x, pandas==y) in requirements.txt and assumes that solves it, ignoring that the crashing transitive dependency still floats unless the whole tree is locked.
Conflates a manifest with a lockfile — treats a requirements.txt containing version ranges (>=, ~=) as if it already pins the build.
Blames it purely on OS/Python/environment differences ('works on my machine') and misses that pip re-resolves versions at install time as the actual cause.
Recommends everyone run `pip install --upgrade` or move to the latest versions, which reintroduces drift instead of fixing reproducibility.

Offers `pip freeze > requirements.txt` as the complete answer without noting it captures the current environment but omits hashes and blurs declared intent with the locked tree, making it fragile as a manifest.
Generates a lockfile but forgets to commit it to version control, so CI and teammates keep resolving dependencies independently.
reference_answer:
The root cause is that `requirements.txt` declares package names without exact version pins, so `pip` resolves each one to the newest release that still satisfies the (open) constraints at the moment it installs. Because your teammate and each fresh CI container install at a different time, they get different versions — and, critically, different *transitive* dependencies (the packages your direct deps pull in). The crash inside a library neither of you imports directly is a newer transitive version that changed behaviour. The build is simply not reproducible.

The distinction that matters: a manifest (e.g. `pyproject.toml`, or a `requirements.in`) states your intent — the direct dependencies and acceptable version ranges, written for humans. A lockfile (`poetry.lock`, `uv.lock`, `Pipfile.lock`, or a `pip-compile`-generated `requirements.txt`) records the exact resolved version of every package in the whole graph — direct and transitive — usually with content hashes, written for machines to reproduce.

The fix: generate a lockfile from the manifest and commit it to git. Everyone and CI then install from the lockfile (`poetry install`, `uv sync`, or `pip install --require-hashes -r requirements.txt`), yielding a byte-identical tree. This works because the exact version and hash of every node is fixed, so there is nothing left for the resolver to choose. Upgrading becomes a deliberate re-lock step, separate from installing.
